newsitem.title: USA: Annan in Washington to heal U.N.-U.S. wounds.
newsitem.headline: Annan in Washington to heal U.N.-U.S. wounds.

text.p: In his first official trip to Washington, Kofi Annan, the new U.N. secretary-general, attempted to convince congressmen that supporting the world body was a good buy if one considered the alternatives.
Washington owes the United Nations $1.3 billion, a sum that is bankrupting the world body.

"War is a failure of diplomacy. If that is indeed correct, than surely diplomacy is a first line of defence," Annan told Minnesota's congressional delegation shortly after his arrival at the start of a three-day trip that will include talks with President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore.
"Perhaps leaders around the world will spend a little less of the money they are putting into defence and armaments" and more into diplomacy, he said.

Annan, a 58-year-old Ghanaian, who has several degrees from American universities, attended Macalester College in St. Paul, Minnesota, when he first came to the United States, the reason he was invited by the delegation.

Sen. Rod Grams, a Republican and member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said he hoped the money owed to the United Nations by Washington "can be paid sometime in the near future. And at least we are on the right track."
He added there was every indication U.N. "reforms were in the offing," to which Annan responded: "There will be reform."
Annan's trip follows at least two years of relentless criticism by conservatives that the United Nations wants to take over the world and is spending U.S. money needlessly.

For Annan, the occasion is a "time for healing," a reference to the scorn heaped on his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, driven from office by the Clinton administration at the end of a five-year term.

"He has only a few months to cement the relationship and get the United States to really take its place among U.N. members and not shoot from the sidelines," one senior U.N. official said. "It is a healing time but not a long one."

Clinton has proposed paying the debt by 1999, with some conditions attached. But whether the Republican-dominated Congress, which cut non-defence foreign aid to a bare minimlum, will agree is another question.
Annan on Thursday was to see Clinton, Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright and National Security Adviser Sandy Berger, among others.

In a bid to improve U.N. relations with Congress, he also has meetings planned with a host of legislators including House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and North Carolina Sen. Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

The wide gap between Democrats and Republicans was illustrated clearly in Helms' article in Foreign Affairs magazine six months ago in which he advocated the United States withdraw from the United Nations unless its budget was slashed more than anticipated so far.
Annan has touted reform as a top priority and plans wide-ranging proposals in the next six months. But he pointedly said reform did not mean massive or "arbitrary" cuts in vital programmes.
Some nations, such as Japan, believe reform should not mean any lowering of dues but the release of funds for development to poor countries.

Since many U.N. bodies are not under the control of the secretary-general but are funded by voluntary contributions, Annan's influence on wide-ranging restructuring is often dependent on approval by member states.

But since the Clinton administration faulted Boutros-Ghali for allegedly not paying enough attention to reform, Annan was left with an albatross of massive change in order to get the United States to participate fully in the United Nations.
